title: Blue bursts of hot young stars
caption: Spiral galaxy IC 5052, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IC 5052 · constellation Pavo · about 25 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Speckled with blue, white and yellow light, this Hubble image shows part of the spiral galaxy IC 5052, seen side-on and surrounded by distant stars and galaxies. Its blue-white glow picks out a narrow, intricate structure. The galaxy lies in Pavo, the Peacock, in the southern sky.

From this edge-on angle it is hard to work out how a spiral is arranged. IC 5052 is in fact a barred spiral, with arms that do not start at the very center but attach to the ends of a straight bar of stars crossing its middle. Roughly two thirds of spirals, the Milky Way among them, have such a bar.

Pale blue bursts along the galaxy's length, partly hidden by winding lanes of darker gas and dust, are pockets of extremely hot newborn stars. Bars are thought to aid their formation by funnelling material inward from the arms toward these stellar nurseries.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.34 x 2.70 arcminutes) and distance (25 million light years), the frame spans roughly 24,000 × 20,000 light-years. Its light set out about 25 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared light captured by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light included is invisible to the eye, and the long exposure brings out faint background galaxies no eye could see.

alt: A narrow, edge-on spiral galaxy speckled with blue, white and yellow light and crossed by dark dust lanes, among distant stars and galaxies.
